title: Do content-based signals in the PR itself separate policy-violating PRs from genuine newcomer PRs?
hypothesis: PRs closed under AI or low-effort policies differ from merged first-time LLVM PRs in cheap content signals visible before review: whether the description links an existing issue (C1), and description length (C2). At least one reaches AUC ≥ 0.75.
uncertainty: Whether any cheap pre-review signal works, now that account-level signals have failed. If content signals fail too, the area should be paused.
procedure: Pre-registered 2026-11-04 before any content data was collected.
Sample: the 240 PRs from exp-followup-engagement-retrospective (120 policy-closed, 120 merged LLVM newcomer PRs). Labels are already known.
For each PR, read the description (body) via the GitHub REST API. It may have been edited after closing, a limitation.
C1: does the description reference an issue (#number, or a GitHub issue URL)? Absence → more suspicious.
C2: description length in words. Direction not assumed: AUC is reported as max(AUC, 1−AUC), with the observed direction stated.
Primary: the better of C1 and C2 by AUC. Also report the share of genuine newcomers flagged at the threshold that flags half the policy-closed PRs.
successCriteria: The better content signal reaches AUC ≥ 0.75 over at least 150 PRs with readable descriptions
failureCriteria: Both content signals have AUC < 0.60 (pause the area's solution search)
resources: GitHub REST API via the Actions token
expectedLearning: Whether triage support can be built on what a PR says, after account-level signals failed.

nextSteps.ifSuccess: Reopen the triage-signal idea with content signals and test them on a second, non-LLVM control group.
nextSteps.ifFailure: Pause the solution search in this area, and record that cheap pre-review signals don't separate low-effort from genuine PRs.

title: Does author follow-up engagement separate policy-rejected PRs from accepted first-time PRs?
hypothesis: Authors of PRs that projects closed as low-effort or AI-policy violations rarely reply to maintainer comments, while first-time contributors whose PRs were merged usually do.
uncertainty: Whether follow-up engagement is a discriminating signal (assumption a1). If it isn't, a comprehension gate adds friction without filtering.
procedure: Pre-registered 2026-11-03, before any outcome data was collected. Revised from the original per-repo design because GitHub search showed only 10 LLVM PRs citing the policy.

Group A (policy-closed): closed, unmerged PRs created 2025-06-01..2026-11-01 whose text or comments cite an AI policy ('AIToolPolicy', 'policy on tool-generated content', 'AI_POLICY.md', or 'AI slop' in comments), pooled across GitHub, up to 120 PRs.
Group B (newcomer-merged): merged llvm/llvm-project PRs from the same period that received LLVM's first-time-contributor greeting, up to 120.
Group C (newcomer-closed, descriptive only): unmerged LLVM newcomer PRs not citing the policy.

For each PR, fetch issue and review comments via the GitHub REST API. Among PRs with at least one comment by a human other than the author (bots excluded), record whether the author replied afterwards, and the time to reply.
Compare reply rates (Wilson 95% intervals) and median reply times. Code: src/experiments/followup-engagement.ts; runs in the 'Run experiment' workflow.
successCriteria: Group A reply rate is at most half of group B's, with at least 30 eligible PRs in each group
failureCriteria: Reply rates of A and B differ by less than 15 percentage points (assumption refuted)
Fewer than 30 eligible PRs in either group (inconclusive)
resources: GitHub REST and search APIs via the Actions GITHUB_TOKEN
expectedLearning: Whether engagement-based gating is worth prototyping, and how much newcomer friction it would cause (via the reply-time distribution of genuine contributors).

nextSteps.ifSuccess: Build a template-question prototype and dogfood it on this repository. Only contact other maintainers with owner approval.
nextSteps.ifFailure: Mark assumption a1 refuted and reject or park the idea. Look for other discriminating signals.

outcome.summary: Pre-registered verdict: inconclusive. Policy-closed PR authors replied 59.8% of the time (52/87, CI 49–69%) versus 90.2% for merged LLVM newcomers (83/92, CI 82–95%): a clear gap, but short of the ≤ 45.1% success threshold. Exploratory within-LLVM comparison: 80.9% vs 90.2%, so engagement alone discriminates weakly.

title: Prospective field test: how often would the alarm fire on real releases?
hypothesis: Across the 400 popular npm packages from exp-npm-publishing-practices, new releases that add an install script or a new dependency are rare enough (≤ 5% of releases) that alerts wouldn't overwhelm maintainers.
uncertainty: Real-world alert volume (false-alarm burden), which retrospective data on malicious releases can't show.
procedure: Pre-registered 2026-11-04 before any monitoring data was collected.
Daily for 28 days, a scheduled workflow lists new versions of the 400 packages published since the previous check (public npm registry).
For each new version, compare with the previous version: install scripts added or changed, new dependencies.
After 28 days, cross-check flagged versions against OpenSSF malicious-packages reports.
Report the alert rate per release and per package-month, and the number of confirmed malicious hits.
successCriteria: At most 5% of new releases trigger an alert, over at least 300 observed releases
failureCriteria: More than 15% of new releases trigger an alert (alert fatigue likely)
expectedLearning: The false-alarm burden in practice. Malicious hits are unlikely in 28 days, so absence of hits is expected and not evidence against the idea.

nextSteps.ifSuccess: Ask the owner to authorize a small maintainer interest test (requires contacting people).
nextSteps.ifFailure: Refine the signal (e.g. only install hooks) before any further work.

title: How many popular npm packages still publish in a way a stolen token could reproduce?
hypothesis: A substantial share (≥ 40%) of popular npm packages' latest releases were published with neither trusted publishing (OIDC) nor staged human approval, so a maintainer-side alarm would still have a large audience.
uncertainty: Whether npm's new protections have already closed most of the gap the alarm targets (assumption a4).
procedure: Pre-registered 2026-11-04 before data collection. A metadata probe of one package (axios) confirmed the fields exist.

Population A (popular): union of the top 250 results of the npm search API (popularity weight 1.0) for the keywords javascript, typescript, react, node, cli and util. Deduplicated, first 400 packages in result order.
Population B (previously hijacked): the 22 campaign-representative packages from exp-publish-anomaly-campaign-replication.
For each package's latest version, read `_npmUser` from the registry: `trustedPublisher` present → OIDC; `approver` present → staged with human approval; neither → token/interactive publish.
Report the shares, with Wilson 95% intervals.
successCriteria: At least 40% of population A's latest releases have neither trusted publishing nor staged approval (the alarm still has a large audience)
failureCriteria: Fewer than 15% have neither (npm's protections already cover most popular packages)
Fewer than 200 packages could be read (inconclusive)
resources: Public npm registry and search API
expectedLearning: How much of the popular npm ecosystem is still exposed to the token-theft route that hit axios, and whether previously hijacked packages changed their publishing after the attack.

nextSteps.ifSuccess: Refine the alarm toward the exposed population, and consider a staged-release review aid that highlights new install hooks at approval time.
nextSteps.ifFailure: Park the standalone alarm. npm's own controls cover most of its audience.

outcome.summary: Pre-registered verdict: supported. 201 of 400 popular npm packages (50.2%, 95% CI 45–55%) published their latest release with neither trusted publishing nor staged approval. Only 31 (7.8%) use staged human approval. 13 of 22 previously hijacked packages still publish with neither. 'Neither' is an upper bound, because interactive 2FA publishes look the same in metadata.

title: Do cheap pre-review signals separate policy-violating PRs from genuine newcomer PRs?
hypothesis: Authors of PRs closed under AI or low-effort policies opened many more PRs across GitHub in the 30 days before their PR than genuine first-time LLVM contributors did, so this one signal separates the groups well (AUC ≥ 0.75).
uncertainty: Whether any cheap, pre-review signal discriminates at all (assumption a1).
procedure: Pre-registered 2026-11-04 before any signal data was collected.
Sample: the 240 PRs from exp-followup-engagement-retrospective (120 policy-closed, 120 merged LLVM newcomer PRs). Labels are already known.
For each PR, read its creation time (GitHub REST API).
Signal S1: number of PRs the author opened across GitHub in the 30 days before the PR (search API, type:pr author:<login> created:<range>).
Signal S2: author account age at PR creation, in days (users API).
Authors whose accounts no longer exist are counted and reported separately, and excluded from the AUC.
Primary: AUC of S1 (higher → policy-closed). Secondary: AUC of S2 (younger → policy-closed). Secondary: S1 AUC within LLVM only.
Report the share of genuine newcomers flagged at the threshold that catches 50% of policy-closed PRs.
successCriteria: S1 AUC ≥ 0.75 over at least 150 PRs with readable authors
failureCriteria: Both S1 and S2 have AUC < 0.60 (cheap signals don't discriminate)
Fewer than 150 PRs with readable authors (inconclusive)
resources: GitHub REST and search APIs via the Actions token
expectedLearning: Whether pre-review triage support (and tools like Fossier) rests on signals that work, and what they would cost genuine newcomers.

nextSteps.ifSuccess: Prototype an advisory triage Action on this repository's own PRs. Any outreach to other projects needs owner authorization.
nextSteps.ifFailure: Reject this idea and note that unvalidated signal-based tools (Fossier) are likely ineffective.

outcome.summary: Pre-registered verdict: inconclusive. The cross-repo PR burst separates the groups only weakly (AUC 0.64; median 6 vs 1 prior PRs), and account age barely at all (AUC 0.54). Catching half of the policy-violating PRs would also flag about 30% of genuine newcomers. Cheap account-level signals aren't a good basis for triage.

title: Campaign-level replication: do independent hijack campaigns carry structural signals?
hypothesis: Across independent npm hijack campaigns (not individual packages), most carry a new-dependency or install-hook signal.
uncertainty: Whether the first experiment's support generalises beyond the single Shai-Hulud wave that dominated its sample.
procedure: Pre-registered 2026-11-03, before any campaign-level data collection.
Population: OpenSSF OSV reports 2024-01-01..2026-11-02 for hijacked legitimate npm packages (at least 10 non-malicious versions).
Group incidents into campaigns: same campaign name in the report, or same publish date and payload description. Take one representative per campaign.
Classify each campaign's mechanism as in exp-publish-anomaly-retrospective. Reuse the same false-positive baseline method.
successCriteria: At least 60% of classifiable campaigns carry a new-dependency or install-hook signal, with at least 15 classifiable campaigns
failureCriteria: Fewer than 40% of classifiable campaigns carry such signals
estimatedTime: half a day of automated analysis
expectedLearning: Whether structural diffing generalises across attackers, or only catches worm-style campaigns.

nextSteps.ifSuccess: Survey vendor offerings for maintainer-side alerts, then prototype on VENTURE's own packages (none yet).
nextSteps.ifFailure: Narrow the idea to worm/install-hook detection or park it.

outcome.summary: Pre-registered verdict: supported. 12 of 15 classifiable independent campaigns (80%, 95% CI 55–93%) added an install-time hook, versus 1.7% of 423 legitimate releases. Caveats: exactly the minimum of 15 classifiable campaigns; 7 campaigns of unknown mechanism (the share could range from 55% to 86%); 3 file-modification campaigns would evade the alarm.

title: Would simple structural diffs have flagged the documented malicious releases?
hypothesis: Each documented malicious release differs from the previous legitimate release by at least one simple structural signal: a new dependency, a new install-time hook or .pth file, or a missing or changed provenance attestation.
uncertainty: Whether compromised-account releases are structurally anomalous (assumption a1). If they look like normal releases, a maintainer alarm can't work.
procedure: Pre-registered before data collection; revised after a metadata-only feasibility probe.

Feasibility probe (2026-11-03T22:46Z): the malicious versions have been removed from npm and PyPI. Archive source: OpenSSF malicious-packages (OSV) reports, which describe the injected mechanism per malicious version (e.g. MAL-2026-2307 axios, MAL-2026-2144 litellm, MAL-2025-190643 @asyncapi/specs).

Population: OSV entries from 2025-06-01 to 2026-11-01 for packages that still have at least 10 non-malicious versions on their registry (hijacked legitimate packages, not typosquats), up to 60 incidents.
Classify each incident's mechanism from the OSV text into: new dependency, new install-time script or hook (.pth, pre/postinstall), modification of existing files only, or unknown.
False positives: for the same npm packages, use public per-version registry metadata to count how often consecutive legitimate releases add a dependency or an install script.
Code goes under src/experiments/ and runs in the 'Run experiment' workflow; raw results are committed under research/experiments/.
successCriteria: At least 60% of classifiable incidents involve a new dependency or install-time hook
Fewer than 10% of legitimate npm releases add a dependency or install script
failureCriteria: Fewer than 40% of classifiable incidents involve such signals (most attacks only modify existing files)
estimatedTime: half a day of automated analysis
resources: Public npm and PyPI registry APIs
expectedLearning: Whether structural anomaly detection is a viable basis for maintainer-side alerts, and its false-positive cost.

nextSteps.ifSuccess: Survey existing vendor offerings for maintainer-side alerts before prototyping.
nextSteps.ifFailure: Reject or park the alarm; investigate behaviour-based detection instead.

outcome.summary: Pre-registered verdict: supported. 58/58 classifiable hijack incidents carried an install-hook signal (95% CI 94–100%), versus 1.3% of 1,119 legitimate releases. Caveat from the independence check: 56 of 60 incidents belong to one Shai-Hulud campaign wave, so this is about 5 independent attacks. Assumption a1 stays untested pending a campaign-level replication (pre-registered).
